卡古爾鼓具有獨特的混合音響特徵。其鋸齒邊緣被刮擊時發出尖銳、刺耳的金屬質感，帶有: The kagul has a particular mixed sound. Scraping the saw-toothed edge gives a sharp, piercing metallic quality, bright and rough, like a scraper or a wind chime. When a beater strikes the face it gives a dull, dry knock in a low register. Used together the two ways of playing make a composite sound with a strong contrast of high and low. It carries strongly and has a somewhat irritating quality, which is exactly its advantage when driving birds from the rice fields. Beside the warm resonance of traditional drums the kagul sounds rawer and more primitive; beside a metal gong its tone is drier and leaner and more directional, so it catches the attention effectively.
卡古爾鼓採用竹製結構為主要材質。鼓身由竹筒製成，具有天然的空心共鳴腔體。鼓的一側: The kagul is made mainly of bamboo. The body is a bamboo tube, which gives a natural hollow resonating chamber. One edge is specially made with a saw-toothed structure that increases the effect of the scraping. The face is of bamboo, or possibly of animal skin, and gives the basic tone when struck. It is played with two beaters, usually of wood, one used for scraping the toothed edge and the other for striking the face. The materials are plain throughout, showing the traditional craft of the indigenous peoples of the southern Philippines.

Its use has changed with circumstance: the Maguindanaon and the Banuwaen used it in the rice fields to drive birds away with its sound, and that use is no longer practised; the Maguindanaon and the Bukidnon also used it on social occasions to play simple dance rhythms, usually a single pattern and sometimes combined with another.

The kagul is a Philippine bamboo scraped slit drum, an idiophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 112.2. It is a bamboo sounding body with a saw-toothed edge on one side, played with two beaters, one scraping the toothed edge and the other striking the beat. The Maguindanaon and the Visayans use it; the Maguindanaon and the Banuwaen used to put it in the rice fields to drive birds away with its sound, a use no longer practised. The Maguindanaon and the Bukidnon also use it on social occasions to accompany simple dance rhythms, usually one rhythm pattern with another now and then.
